section.title: The Covenant at Shechem
section.sectionRationale: The book ends where the faith of Israel is put to its sharpest test: a covenant renewal at Shechem. Joshua rehearses the whole story of God's grace, from Abraham to the conquest, all of it God's doing, and then presses the decision: choose this day whom you will serve. The people vow to serve the LORD, a stone is set up as witness, and the book closes with the deaths of Joshua, Joseph's long-carried bones, and Eleazar. It is one movement, the covenant at Shechem, the climactic call to serve the LORD alone in response to His grace.
section.thesis: Because the LORD did everything, taking Abraham, redeeming Israel, giving a land they did not toil for, the only fitting response is to fear and serve Him alone, so Joshua summons the people to a deliberate, witnessed choice, and closes the book with a settled people, a buried patriarch's fulfilled hope, and a covenant sealed by grace.
section.frameNote: Four beats: God's mighty acts rehearsed from Abraham to the conquest, verses 1 to 13; the call to choose whom to serve and the people's vow, verses 14 to 24; the covenant sealed with a stone of witness, verses 25 to 28; and the closing deaths and burials, verses 29 to 33.

units.label: God's mighty acts rehearsed
units.note: I took, I gave, I brought, I sent, all of grace

verses.text: Then Joshua assembled all the tribes of Israel at Shechem. He summoned the elders, leaders, judges, and officers of Israel, and they presented themselves before God.

And Joshua said to all the people, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Long ago your fathers, including Terah the father of Abraham and Nahor, lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods.
But I took your father Abraham from beyond the Euphrates and led him through all the land of Canaan, and I multiplied his descendants. I gave him Isaac,
and to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. I gave Esau Mount Seir to possess, but Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt.
Then I sent Moses and Aaron, and I afflicted the Egyptians by what I did there, and afterward I brought you out.
When I brought your fathers out of Egypt and you reached the Red Sea, the Egyptians pursued them with chariots and horsemen as far as the Red Sea.

So your fathers cried out to the LORD, and He put darkness between you and the Egyptians, over whom He brought the sea and engulfed them. Your very eyes saw what I did to the Egyptians. Then you lived in the wilderness for a long time.

Later, I brought you to the land of the Amorites who lived beyond the Jordan. They fought against you, but I delivered them into your hand, that you should possess their land when I destroyed them before you.
Then Balak son of Zippor, the king of Moab, set out to fight against Israel. He sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse you,
but I would not listen to Balaam. So he blessed you again and again, and I delivered you from his hand.

After this, you crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho. The people of Jericho fought against you, as did the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites, and Jebusites, and I delivered them into your hand.
I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove out the two Amorite kings before you, but not by your own sword or bow.
So I gave you a land on which you did not toil and cities that you did not build, and now you live in them and eat from vineyards and olive groves that you did not plant.’

units.label: Choose whom you will serve
units.note: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD

verses.text: Now, therefore, fear the LORD and serve Him in sincerity and truth; cast aside the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and serve the LORD.

But if it is unpleasing in your sight to serve the LORD, then {{bachar|choose}} for yourselves this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living. As for me and my house, we will {{abad|serve}} the LORD!”
The people replied, “Far be it from us to forsake the LORD to serve other gods!

For the LORD our God brought us and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, and performed these great signs before our eyes. He also protected us throughout our journey and among all the nations through which we traveled.
And the LORD drove out before us all the nations, including the Amorites who lived in the land. We too will serve the LORD, because He is our God!”
But Joshua said to the people, “You are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God; He is a jealous God; He will not forgive your rebellion or your sins.
If you forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods, He will turn and bring disaster on you and consume you, even after He has been good to you.”
“No!” replied the people. “We will serve the LORD!”
Then Joshua told them, “You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD.” “We are witnesses!” they said.
“Now, therefore,” he said, “get rid of the foreign gods among you and incline your hearts to the LORD, the God of Israel.”
So the people said to Joshua, “We will serve the LORD our God and obey His voice.”

units.label: The covenant sealed with a stone of witness
units.note: this stone will be a witness against us

verses.text: On that day Joshua made a {{berit|covenant}} for the people, and there at Shechem he established for them a statute and ordinance.
Joshua recorded these things in the Book of the Law of God. Then he took a large stone and set it up there under the oak that was near the sanctuary of the LORD.

And Joshua said to all the people, “You see this stone. It will be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us, and it will be a witness against you if you ever deny your God.”
Then Joshua sent the people away, each to his own inheritance.

units.label: The closing deaths and burials
units.note: Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua

verses.text: Some time later, Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110.
And they buried him in the land of his inheritance, at Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.
Israel had served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him and who had experienced all the works that the LORD had done for Israel.

And the bones of Joseph, which the Israelites had brought up out of Egypt, were buried at Shechem in the plot of land that Jacob had purchased from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for a hundred pieces of silver. So it became an inheritance for Joseph’s descendants.
Eleazar son of Aaron also died, and they buried him at Gibeah, which had been given to his son Phinehas in the hill country of Ephraim.

bachar.gloss: To choose, select, decide for. Joshua calls Israel to bachar this day whom they will serve. The word presses for a deliberate, conscious decision; there is no drifting into covenant loyalty. Yet the deeper truth of the book is that God first chose Israel, taking Abraham by grace, so their choosing is a response to His prior choice, an answering of grace with allegiance.

abad.gloss: To serve, worship, work for. The verb sounds like a refrain through the chapter: serve the LORD, whom will you serve, we will serve the LORD. To abad the LORD is to give Him exclusive worship and obedient allegiance, the opposite of serving other gods. The whole covenant renewal turns on whom Israel will serve, and Joshua models the answer: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

berit.gloss: Covenant, a binding, sworn relationship. Joshua cuts a berit for the people at Shechem, renewing their bond with the LORD, complete with statutes, a written record, and a stone of witness. The covenant frames Israel's whole life as a sworn relationship with God, one that Israel could not finally keep, pointing ahead to the new covenant secured in Christ.

basic.context: The book climaxes with a covenant renewal at Shechem, the place where Abraham first built an altar in the land. Joshua speaks for God and retells the whole story of Israel, and the striking thing is that almost every verb has God as its subject: I took Abraham, I gave, I brought you out, I sent, I delivered, I gave you a land you did not toil for. It is grace from beginning to end. On that basis, Joshua presses the decision: choose today whom you will serve, and he declares his own resolve, as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD. The people vow to serve the LORD; Joshua soberly warns they are not able to serve a holy God on their own, yet they insist, and he makes them witnesses against themselves. A covenant is sealed and a stone set up as witness. The book ends with the deaths of Joshua and Eleazar and the burial of Joseph's bones, carried up from Egypt at last. The question underneath is: how will God's people respond to a lifetime of grace?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative recording a covenant ceremony, the theological summit of the book. The rehearsal of God's acts grounds the call to serve Him in grace, not merit. Joshua's warning that they are not able to serve the LORD is a sober note about human inability that points beyond the old covenant to the need for a new heart. We read the famous choose this day within its context of response to God's prior, saving initiative.
basic.originalLanguages: Joshua calls Israel to bachar, to choose, whom they will abad, serve; the verb serve rings through the chapter. On that day he cuts a berit, a covenant, for the people, sealed by a stone of witness.
basic.typology: Joseph's bones, carried from Egypt and buried in the land at last, are faith's fulfillment, a man who died trusting God's promise and is finally brought home. Joshua leading Israel to serve the LORD in the land points to the greater Joshua who brings His people into the true inheritance and enables their service.
basic.christ: Joshua's sober word, you are not able to serve the LORD, exposes a need the old covenant could not meet, and it points to Christ, who serves the Father perfectly, bears our covenant-breaking, and gives a new heart. The whole grace-drenched history Joshua recounts culminates in Christ, God's greatest I took, I gave, I sent, sending His Son to redeem His people.
basic.god: God is the God of sovereign grace, the acting subject of Israel's whole story; everything they have is His gift. He is holy and jealous, worthy of exclusive service. And He is faithful, keeping His promises across generations, so that even Joseph's centuries-old hope is honored. Grace, holiness, and faithfulness meet in Him.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 50 records Joseph's dying charge that his bones be carried to the land. Deuteronomy 30 sets before Israel life and death, blessing and curse, urging them to choose life. Jeremiah 31 promises the new covenant. And Hebrews 11 lists Joseph's faith about his bones among the heroes of faith.
basic.oneStory: At Shechem, Joshua rehearses the whole history of God's grace and calls Israel to choose to serve the LORD alone, sealing a covenant sealed by grace. The book closes with a settled people, a covenant renewed, and Joseph's long-carried bones buried at last, faith fulfilled. It all points to Christ, the culmination of God's saving acts, who keeps the covenant His people could not and brings them home.

context.literary:
Chapter 24 follows the shape of an ancient treaty almost point for point: a historical prologue recounting the great king's past benefits, verses 2 to 13; stipulations and a demand for exclusive loyalty, verses 14 to 24; provisions for the covenant document and a witness, verses 25 to 28; and here, unusually, a narrative epilogue of deaths and burials, verses 29 to 33, that formally closes not just the ceremony but the entire book. Ancient treaties regularly listed witnesses, often the gods of both parties; this chapter cannot do that, since there is only one God, so a stone takes the place other treaties gave to a god, it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us, personifying the witness function no other party could fill.

The prologue's rhetoric is unusually relentless: nearly every clause has God as its subject, I took, I gave, I multiplied, I sent, I delivered, repeated so many times across verses 3 to 13 that a hearer cannot come away with any other impression than that Israel's entire history, land, deliverance, and even its enemies' defeat, belongs to God's action rather than its own. Only after this saturation of divine verbs does the speech pivot, now therefore, to what Israel must do, a literary order, grace first, then obligation, that shapes the whole speech's logic.
context.historical:
Shechem was already the most covenant-saturated site in Israel's memory before Joshua ever gathered anyone there. Abram built his first altar in the land at the oak of Moreh near Shechem, Genesis 12:6 to 7; Jacob bought land there and set up his own altar, Genesis 33:18 to 20; and Jacob later buried his household's foreign gods under an oak near Shechem before leading his family to Bethel, Genesis 35:2 to 4, an act this chapter's own demand, get rid of the foreign gods among you, verse 23, echoes almost exactly, at almost the very same spot. Israel had also already renewed the covenant at nearby Mount Ebal under Joshua himself, chapter 8, reading the whole law before the assembled nation between Ebal and Gerizim. Choosing Shechem again for the final ceremony was choosing the most rehearsed covenant ground in the land.

The treaty form of the speech, historical prologue followed by an exclusive loyalty demand, matches known ancient Near Eastern political documents in which a great king recounted benefits already given before requiring loyalty in return, a form Israel's hearers, familiar with such documents from surrounding empires, would have recognized instantly as formal and binding, not merely ceremonial words. Joseph's bones, carried through four centuries of slavery, wilderness, and conquest, are finally buried in the very plot Jacob had purchased there, Genesis 33:19, a promise, Genesis 50:25, kept across a longer span of time than almost any other in the Old Testament.
context.canonical:
Israel's history quietly turns Shechem's meaning against itself in the very period this book's epilogue anticipates. Within roughly two centuries, Abimelech is made king beside the same oak and pillar at Shechem, Judges 9:6, funded by silver from the temple of Baal-berith, the exact site of covenant loyalty to the LORD becoming, in one generation, the site of a coup funded by a rival god. And when the united kingdom splits, it is to Shechem that all Israel goes to make Rehoboam king, 1 Kings 12:1, only to tear the kingdom in two there instead. The place where Israel once said with one voice, we will serve the LORD, becomes, twice over, the place where Israel's unity actually breaks.

The chapter's central summons, choose this day whom you will serve, becomes one of Scripture's most repeated calls to decision, echoed in Elijah's how long will you waver between two opinions, if the LORD is God, follow Him, 1 Kings 18:21, and in Moses' own earlier charge to choose life, Deuteronomy 30:19. And Joseph's bones, honored here after centuries of waiting, are remembered by the writer of Hebrews among the great acts of faith, by faith Joseph, when his end was near, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions concerning his bones, Hebrews 11:22, treating an old man's dying instruction about his own bones as evidence of real confidence in a promise he would not live to see kept.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author's central purpose is to ground every demand in prior grace so thoroughly that no reader could mistake obedience for the price of the relationship rather than its response. By making God the subject of nearly every verb in the historical review, he forecloses any reading in which Israel earns, contributes to, or partly causes its own deliverance; the intent is that gratitude, not obligation, should be the emotional engine behind the choice Joshua then demands.

A second purpose is to make that choice unmistakably deliberate and witnessed rather than vague or merely emotional. Joshua presses the people three times, forces them to answer aloud twice, and then names them witnesses against themselves, verse 22, precisely so that no one could later claim ignorance or ambush; the ceremony is built to be legally, not merely spiritually, binding, complete with a written record and a physical monument.

A final purpose emerges in Joshua's own blunt interruption, you are not able to serve the LORD, verse 19, spoken directly after the people's confident vow. The author wants this warning on record before the closing narrative of deaths and burials, so that the book cannot be read as ending on human resolve; it must end, instead, on a resolve immediately shown to be fragile, setting up everything that follows in Judges.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The precise covenant ceremony, its Shechem location, its stone, its written record in a specific book, describes a one-time event; no community today needs to reenact a treaty ritual to belong to God. What does transfer is the ceremony's underlying logic, which functions as a pattern rather than a procedure: grace recounted first, response demanded second, and the response made deliberate and accountable rather than left vague. A church or a believer renewing commitment to Christ is not required to set up a stone, but is well served by Joshua's instinct that vague, undocumented resolve rarely survives pressure.

Joshua's warning, you are not able to serve the LORD, is descriptive of a real spiritual condition rather than a prescription never to try; it functions the way the law itself functions for Paul, exposing inability so that grace, not effort, becomes the only remaining hope, a diagnosis meant to drive readers toward dependence rather than toward giving up on obedience altogether.

debates.question: Why does Joshua say, you are not able to serve the LORD, right after the people vow to do so?

views.label: A sober exposure of human inability apart from grace
views.case: Joshua confronts a glib, self-confident vow with the holiness and jealousy of God and the people's proven bent to idolatry; he is not forbidding them to serve God but stripping away presumption, showing that serving a holy God is beyond mere human resolve, a truth that drives toward the need for a new heart and points to the new covenant, Jeremiah 31:33.

views.label: A rhetorical test to deepen their commitment
views.case: By pushing back against their easy answer, Joshua forces the people to count the cost and reaffirm their choice more soberly, verses 21 to 24, so the warning functions to make their commitment deliberate and witnessed rather than casual, guarding against the shallow enthusiasm that would soon collapse in Judges.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree Joshua refuses cheap, presumptuous commitment: serving the holy LORD is no light thing, and the people's inability, soon proved in Judges, points beyond the old covenant to the grace and new heart God gives in Christ.

debates.question: Are the days of the Judges, and later the exile, proof that the covenant made here at Shechem simply failed, or that it did exactly what a covenant is meant to do?

views.label: A tragic failure, later remedied by a wholly new covenant
views.case: The people's vow collapses within a generation, Judges 2:11 to 13, and the disaster of exile eventually falls exactly as later covenant curses warned; on this reading Shechem's covenant was a genuine but ultimately unsuccessful arrangement, its failure being precisely why Jeremiah later announces a covenant that will not be like the one their fathers broke, Jeremiah 31:32, a deliberately different, better kind of covenant rather than a repair of the old one.

views.label: A covenant that functioned exactly as covenants function, exposing rather than preventing sin
views.case: Paul teaches that the law given at Sinai served in part to make sin fully known and to multiply the trespass, Romans 5:20; on this reading the Shechem covenant's collapse was not a design flaw but part of its intended role, demonstrating conclusively, through Israel's own history, that no covenant resting on human resolve alone could ever be kept, preparing the ground for grace to be seen for what it actually is.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that human resolve proved insufficient and that the eventual answer lies outside the old covenant altogether, in a new covenant secured by God's own initiative rather than Israel's promise; they differ mainly on whether that insufficiency was a surprise within the story or always, in some sense, the story's own point.

study.originalLanguages:
Bachar, abad, and berit already anchor the lexicon; three further details deepen the chapter's Hebrew texture.

The command in verse 14 pairs fear the LORD, yare, with serve Him, abad, a standard biblical pairing, Deuteronomy 10:12 uses the identical combination, since fear here does not mean terror but the reverent, worshipful awe that produces obedient service rather than paralysis; Joshua is not asking Israel to be afraid of God so much as to take Him with the seriousness His greatness deserves.

The refrain elohim acherim, other gods or foreign gods, sounds through the speech like a drumbeat, verses 2, 14, 15, 16, 20, and 23, always as the thing to be cast aside or gotten rid of rather than merely avoided; the demand in verse 14, cast aside, is a strong, physical term, the same kind of decisive removal Jacob demanded of his own household at this very location generations earlier, get rid of the foreign gods that are among you, Genesis 35:2, so that Joshua's demand is not an innovation but a return to a standard already set at Shechem itself.

Joseph's burial plot was purchased, Genesis 33:19, for a hundred pieces of silver, in Hebrew kesitah, a monetary unit so obscure that its exact value was already uncertain by the time later translators rendered it, appearing in only a small handful of places in the entire Hebrew Bible; that a chapter otherwise dense with covenant vocabulary, choose, serve, covenant, closes on a word this rare and this tied to one family's centuries-old promise is itself a quiet signal that God's faithfulness reaches even into details too small and too old for most of Israel to still remember clearly.

Finally, incline your hearts, verse 23, uses lev, heart, the Hebrew Bible's word for the whole inner self, will and mind together rather than mere emotion; Joshua does not ask for outward compliance alone but for the same organ of decision that has, throughout the chapter, been asked to choose.

Fear, serve, cast aside, heart, and an old, nearly forgotten coin: the vocabulary of this last chapter reaches for both the grand covenant language of choose and serve and the smallest domestic details of clearing a house of idols and paying an old debt in full, as if Scripture wants readers to know that God's faithfulness operates at both scales at once.

typology.type: Joseph's bones carried from Egypt and buried in the land
typology.fulfillment: Joseph, near death in Egypt, made Israel swear an oath about bones he would not need for four centuries, by faith, Hebrews calls it, when his end was near, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions concerning his bones, Hebrews 11:22. Their burial here, in ground his own father had purchased generations earlier, closes a promise kept across more time than almost any other in Scripture, and quietly anticipates the resurrection hope Paul later grounds in Christ, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The type escalates because Joseph's bones needed centuries and other people's obedience to reach the land, while the resurrection body Christ secures needs no one else's faithfulness to be raised on the day appointed.

typology.type: Joshua leading Israel to serve the LORD in the inheritance
typology.fulfillment: Joshua, whose very name means the LORD saves, brings a redeemed people into the land God swore, then presses them to serve Him there in gratitude rather than obligation. The greater Joshua, Jesus, carries the identical name into the New Testament and brings His people into a Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4:8 to 9, then works in them both to will and to act according to His good purpose, Philippians 2:13. The type escalates because the first Joshua could only lead people to a border and press them to choose service by their own resolve, while the greater Joshua both brings His people in and supplies, from within, the very obedience He asks for.

typology.type: A covenant Israel vowed but could not keep
typology.fulfillment: The people answer Joshua's warning with a vow made not once but twice, we will serve the LORD, verses 21 and 24, only for Judges to record that within a generation they served the Baals instead, 2:11 to 13. Jeremiah names the flaw directly, not like the covenant I made with their fathers, a covenant they broke, and promises instead one written on the heart rather than merely spoken aloud, Jeremiah 31:31 to 33. The type escalates from a covenant whose success depended entirely on a people's own remembered resolve, resolve this very chapter shows evaporating with striking speed, to a covenant whose success depends entirely on God's own unbreakable resolve to complete what He begins.

typology.type: A public, witnessed choice to serve the LORD
typology.fulfillment: Joshua will not accept a private or ambiguous decision; he forces the people to speak their choice aloud, twice, and then declares them witnesses against themselves, verse 22, converting an inward disposition into an outward, accountable act with consequences attached. Paul asks for the same kind of decisive, spoken commitment from every believer, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved, Romans 10:9. The type escalates because Israel's spoken vow proved unable to secure the loyalty it declared, while the confession Paul describes rests not on the strength of the speaker's own resolve but on the resurrection already accomplished before anyone speaks a word.

study.christ:
The whole ceremony at Shechem is built on a single, relentless truth, that salvation runs entirely from God to His people rather than the reverse, and that truth finds its highest expression in Christ. Joshua's rehearsal of history is a torrent of first person divine verbs, I took your father Abraham, I gave him Isaac, I sent Moses and Aaron, I delivered you, I gave you a land you did not toil for, verses 3 to 13, and this same grammar of grace reaches its climax generations later in a single greater gift, God so loved the world that He gave His only Son, John 3:16, the ultimate entry in a list of divine giving that this chapter's own list was always, in its own smaller way, anticipating.

Joshua's blunt interruption, you are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God, verse 19, is not a contradiction of the call to serve but the very diagnosis the gospel answers. Israel's later history proves the diagnosis correct; within a generation the vow collapses, Judges 2:11 to 13. Christ answers exactly this inability, not by lowering the standard of holy service but by supplying it Himself, He was Himself faithful over God's house as a son, Hebrews 3:6, and offers His own perfect obedience in place of the obedience Israel could vow but not sustain.

Joseph's bones, carried for four centuries and finally buried in ground bought long before by faith rather than by sight, testify that God's promises outlast the patience of every generation that must wait for them, a hope 1 Corinthians 15:20 grounds fully in the risen Christ, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, the pledge that everyone else who trusts Him will follow. And the stone Joshua sets up to witness against the people if they ever deny their God anticipates a witness of a very different kind, the Spirit Himself testifying with our spirit that we are children of God, Romans 8:16, a witness that no longer merely accuses but assures. Choose this day whom you will serve finds its truest, final answer not in a decision Israel could make and unmake, but in the One who first chose, and kept, His people.
study.god:
God appears here as the sole and total agent of His people's entire history, a portrait this chapter draws with unusual insistence. Every major turn, Abraham's call, Isaac's birth, the exodus, the defeat of Pharaoh, the crossing of the sea, the defeat of the Amorite kings, is narrated with God Himself as the one acting, I took, I gave, I sent, I delivered, so that by the time Joshua reaches now therefore in verse 14, the hearer has no honest ground left for thinking Israel's obedience could ever be a form of repayment; it can only ever be response.

He is also holy and jealous in a way Joshua states as bluntly as anywhere in the Old Testament, He is a holy God, He is a jealous God, He will not forgive your rebellion or your sins, verse 19, language meant not to frighten Israel away from serving Him but to strip away any casual assumption that serving Him is a light or easily managed commitment; a God this great does not accept careless devotion.

He is patient across scales of time that dwarf ordinary human memory, honoring, in this very chapter, an oath Joseph extracted from his family four hundred years earlier, before slavery, before Moses, before the exodus had even begun, Genesis 50:24 to 25. A God who keeps a promise about a burial plot for four centuries is a God whose patience with His people's slower failures should not be mistaken for indifference to them.

And He is a God who, having demanded a response He knows His people cannot fully sustain, does not walk away from the shortfall. The tension this chapter leaves open, a vow the people cannot keep from a God who will not overlook the breaking of it, is not this chapter's final word; it is the very tension the rest of Scripture exists to resolve, not by lowering what holiness requires, but by God Himself, in Christ, becoming both the sacrifice for the breach and the power behind the obedience He first demanded.

crossReferences.note: Abram's very first altar in the promised land stood at the oak of Moreh near Shechem, built the moment the LORD first told him, I will give this land to your offspring. The covenant ceremony that finally closes the conquest, centuries later, returns Israel to the exact place where the promise to their father Abraham first took visible shape.

Long before Joshua ever demanded it, Jacob had already told his own household, get rid of the foreign gods that are among you, and buried them under the very oak near Shechem this chapter later mentions. Joshua's identical demand at the identical site shows Israel being called back to a standard its own ancestor had already set there.

Dying in Egypt, Joseph made the Israelites swear an oath that they would carry his bones out of Egypt when God eventually visited them, an oath made roughly four centuries before Joshua 24:32 records it finally being kept, one of the longest fulfilled promises recorded anywhere in Scripture.

Moses had already set before Israel this same choice in almost the same words, see, I have set before you today life and prosperity, death and adversity, therefore choose life. Joshua's choose this day whom you will serve is not a new demand invented at Shechem but Moses' own dying charge, renewed for a new generation standing in the land at last.

Generations later, Elijah confronts a divided nation with the identical structure of demand, how long will you waver between two opinions, if the LORD is God, follow Him, but if Baal, then follow him, showing that the choice Joshua forced into the open at Shechem never actually stayed settled for long.

Within roughly two centuries, Abimelech is made king beside the oak and the pillar at Shechem, funded by silver taken from the temple of Baal-berith. The very site where all Israel once vowed together, we will serve the LORD, becomes the site of a coup financed by a rival god.

When the united kingdom fractures after Solomon's death, it is to Shechem that all Israel gathers to make Rehoboam king, only for the assembly to end in division rather than renewal. The place of Israel's most unified yes becomes, a second time, the place of its worst no.

God promises a covenant unlike the one Israel's fathers broke after Shechem, one written directly on the heart rather than spoken aloud and then forgotten. The gap this chapter leaves open, a vow the people make but cannot keep, is precisely the gap this promised covenant is designed to close.

Joseph, near the end of his life in Egypt, is remembered among the heroes of faith for a single act, giving instructions concerning his bones, confident of a promise he would never live to see kept. His burial in this chapter, four centuries later, is the quiet proof that his confidence was not misplaced.

Paul asks for the same kind of decisive, spoken commitment Joshua demanded at Shechem, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, you will be saved, though resting now on a foundation Israel's own vow never had, the finished, unrepeatable work of a risen Christ rather than a people's own remembered resolve.

study.oneStory:
Genesis had already made Shechem a place where households got rid of foreign gods before drawing near to God, Jacob and his family burying theirs under an oak there generations before Joshua ever stood on the same ground, Genesis 35:2 to 4. That this final national covenant returns to the same soil is no accident; the whole book of Joshua has been leading Israel back to where the promise to Abraham first took visible shape, an altar at Shechem, Genesis 12:6 to 7, so that the conquest ends exactly where the promise began, land actually possessed at last, standing on the very spot where it was first spoken.

The covenant made here does not, in the end, hold, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise; within two centuries the same site hosts a coup crowned beside its sacred oak, Judges 9:6, and later still, the whole kingdom gathers there only to split apart instead of renew, 1 Kings 12:1. Shechem, the place of Israel's most emphatic yes, becomes, twice over, the place of its worst division, and the honesty of that outcome is itself part of what the Bible is telling its readers, that human resolve, however sincerely vowed under however sacred a stone, was never going to be the mechanism by which God's people would finally be kept faithful.

What this chapter can only demand, choose this day whom you will serve, and cannot supply, the resolve to actually keep that choice, the rest of Scripture goes on to promise and finally deliver. A new covenant, written not on stone but on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33. A Mediator who serves the Father perfectly where every human mediator before Him eventually failed, Hebrews 3:6. And Joseph's long-buried hope, honored here after four centuries, becomes the pattern for every promise still unfulfilled at the end of this book, and at the end of every reader's own life, that the God who kept His word about one man's bones can be trusted to keep His word about everything else He has ever promised, including a resurrection and a land that will, this time, never need to be conquered again, Revelation 21:1 to 4.

quiz.q: What is striking about how Joshua retells Israel's history at Shechem?

options.text: Nearly every action is God's: I took, I gave, I brought out, I sent, showing salvation is all of grace.
options.note: Verses 2 to 13 make God the acting subject throughout, grounding the call in grace.

options.text: It focuses on Israel's own achievements and strength.
options.note: The opposite: the emphasis is on God's acts, not Israel's achievements; even the land was one they did not toil for.

options.text: It centers on Joshua's personal leadership.
options.note: Joshua points to God's acts, not his own leadership, as the story's driving force.

options.text: It omits the exodus and the conquest.
options.note: It recounts the exodus, wilderness, and conquest in detail as God's mighty acts.

quiz.q: What decision did Joshua press upon the people?

options.text: To choose that day whom they would serve, and to serve the LORD alone.
options.note: Verses 14 to 15 call for a deliberate choice; Joshua vows, as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

options.text: To choose a new leader to succeed him.
options.note: The choice was about whom to serve, God or idols, not about a successor.

options.text: To decide which land each tribe would take.
options.note: The land was already divided; the choice here was whom they would serve.

options.text: To vote on whether to keep the covenant law.
options.note: It was a call to serve the LORD wholeheartedly, not a vote on the law.

quiz.q: Why did Joshua warn, you are not able to serve the LORD?

options.text: To confront glib presumption with God's holiness, exposing that serving Him is beyond mere human resolve.
options.note: Verse 19 sobers their easy vow, pointing to the need for a new heart.

options.text: To tell them God did not want their service at all.
options.note: God did want their service; Joshua was exposing their inability apart from grace, not rejecting them.

options.text: Because he doubted God could help them.
options.note: Joshua doubted their self-confident resolve, not God's power; the issue was human inability.

options.text: To encourage them to serve other gods instead.
options.note: The opposite: he urged them to serve the LORD alone and put away foreign gods.

quiz.q: How does the burial of Joseph's bones close the book meaningfully?

options.text: It fulfills Joseph's centuries-old hope, showing God keeps His promises across generations, even through death.
options.note: Verse 32 fulfills Genesis 50:25, a testimony to God's faithfulness and faith's hope.

options.text: It shows the Israelites had forgotten their history.
options.note: The opposite: they remembered and fulfilled Joseph's charge, honoring the promise.

options.text: It proves Joseph had no real faith in God's promise.
options.note: Joseph's charge about his bones was an act of faith in the promise, honored here, Hebrews 11:22.

options.text: It has nothing to do with God's faithfulness.
options.note: It is a powerful sign of God's faithfulness, fulfilling a promise made four centuries earlier.

quiz.q: How does the covenant at Shechem point to Christ?

options.text: God's initiating grace and the covenant Israel could not keep point to Christ, who keeps it, bears its curse, and gives a new heart.
options.note: The grace-based call and human inability point to the new covenant in Christ, Jeremiah 31:33.

options.text: It teaches that people keep covenant with God by willpower alone.
options.note: Israel's later failure shows willpower is not enough; the answer is Christ and the new heart He gives.

options.text: It shows God's grace ended with the conquest.
options.note: God's grace continues and culminates in Christ, the greatest of His saving acts.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The grace-drenched history and the unkept covenant point clearly to Christ and the new covenant.

questions: Joshua grounded the call to serve God in all that God had graciously done. How does remembering God's grace to you fuel your own desire to serve Him?
Choose this day whom you will serve is a call to a deliberate decision, not drifting. Is there any area where you are drifting rather than consciously choosing to serve the LORD?
Joshua declared, as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD. What would it look like for you to lead your own household or sphere in serving God?
Joshua soberly said the people were not able to serve a holy God on their own. How does honestly facing your own inability drive you to depend on Christ and the new heart He gives?
Joseph's bones were carried for centuries until God's promise was fulfilled. What long-awaited promise of God are you holding onto, and how does His proven faithfulness strengthen your hope?

translationNotes.note: Beyond the Euphrates renders a phrase the BSB footnote gives as beyond the River; it recurs in verses 3, 14, and 15, recalling that Abraham's family had worshiped other gods before God called him.
The hornet that drove out the enemy renders an image, echoing Exodus 23:28, of God's own power, not by your own sword or bow, winning the land.
The oak near the sanctuary is rendered terebinth in the BSB footnote; Shechem was long associated with covenant, from Abraham's altar, Genesis 12:6-7.
A hundred pieces of silver renders a hundred kesitahs, an ancient unit whose exact value is no longer known, as the BSB footnote notes; the burial fulfills Joseph's charge in Genesis 50:25.
